column4: The section uses 41:50 as a crooked account of favor, where the speaker says “هذا لي.” Its neighbor 41:51 adds the response after a gift—turning away—and after harm—making extended supplication—completing the contrast with telling of the Lord's favor.

The section says the three gifts include guidance and commands that the Lord's favor be told. The people of Paradise say “الحمد لله الذي هدانا لهذا” and acknowledge they would not have been guided without God; this voices guidance as a gift from its giver.

The section commands the recipient to tell of the Lord's favor. Qarun's people tell him to use what God granted for the Hereafter and “أحسن كما أحسن الله إليك”; this gives an explicit response to received favor that contrasts with claiming it as one's own in 28:78.

The section calls “هذا لي” a false account of favor. Qarun answers his people's reminder that God granted him wealth by claiming it came from his own knowledge (“على علم عندي”); neighboring 28:77 supplies the reminder he rejects.

The section commands “فلا تنهر” toward the asker. 18:28 likewise says not to drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening (“ولا تطرد الذين يدعون ربهم”), directly extending protection to devoted seekers.

Like 18:28, this ayah forbids driving away people who call on their Lord (“ولا تطرد الذين يدعون ربهم”). It gives a second direct counterpart to the section's command not to rebuke the person who comes seeking.

The section allows “السائل” to be a person who comes with a question. 58:1 recounts a woman pleading and disputing her case with the Prophet, and says God hears their exchange; this is a petitioner whose speech receives attention.

The section recalls Moses' request and God's answer in 20:36. Here Moses, in need, says “إني لما أنزلت إلي من خير فقير”; the prayer for whatever good God sends makes the speaker both a petitioner and a recipient of provision.

The section includes a prayer answered with “قد أوتيت سؤلك” and God's promise of nearness to the caller. 40:60 gives the direct call-and-response formulation, “ادعوني أستجب لكم,” as another statement that a seeker may address God and receive an answer.

The section's examples include God answering a questioner and Moses receiving what he asked. 27:62 asks who answers the distressed person when he calls and removes hardship; it makes divine response to the needy caller explicit.

The section gives Moses' words about the favor bestowed on him and examples of remembering divine gifts. Here a person asks God to enable gratitude for the favor given to him and his parents (“أن أشكر نعمتك”), turning recognition of favor into spoken prayer.
The section connects telling a Lord's favor with voiced acknowledgment. Solomon asks God to enable him to be grateful for “نعمتك التي أنعمت علي”; this is a direct spoken response to a received favor.

The section contrasts telling that a gift belongs to the Lord with the claim “هذا لي” in 41:50. In 18:39 the companion tells the garden owner to say “ما شاء الله لا قوة إلا بالله,” a specific correction to self-reliance when entering a place of wealth.

The section says the material “السائل” at the door is protected from rebuke. 76:8 depicts believers feeding a needy person, an orphan, and a captive, putting vulnerable recipients in the scene of giving.

After 76:8 names those being fed, this ayah gives the feeders' words: “إنما نطعمكم لوجه الله” and says they seek neither repayment nor thanks. Their speech shows care for recipients without pressure or injury.

The section ties asking for help to the Lord's provision. This neighbor to 2:273 says whatever good people spend is for themselves and will be repaid to them; it completes the context in which the next ayah describes poor people who need support.

The section asks the speaker to tell of the Lord's favor. When travelers mount what carries them, they are taught to say that God subjected it and that they could not have controlled it (“سبحان الذي سخر لنا هذا”); the words identify the giver of a received benefit.
This neighbor completes the spoken acknowledgment begun in 43:13: “وإنا إلى ربنا لمنقلبون.” The speaker names return to the Lord after acknowledging the transport as God's gift.
The section's command is to voice recognition of the Lord's favor. The people of Paradise say “الحمد لله الذي أذهب عنا الحزن,” directly voicing thanks for a deliverance they have received.
This neighbor completes the praise in 35:34 by naming God's grace as the reason they were settled in the lasting home (“من فضله”). It adds the specific favor behind their spoken thanks.

The section says “سأل” includes asking about something. This ayah explicitly says people ask the Prophet for a ruling about women and orphans; the reply attends to their rights, a concrete inquiry met with guidance.

The opening “يستفتونك” presents people asking the Prophet for a ruling about inheritance, and he answers them. It is another specific instance of the knowledge-seeker included by the section's broad sense of “السائل.”

The section notes that asking may be reciprocal (“تساءلوا”). 37:50 shows the people of Paradise turning toward one another to ask; 37:51 begins one speaker's account, bringing the section's mutual questioning and telling together.
This neighbor continues the mutual conversation in 37:50: one of them begins, “إني كان لي قرين.” Its own contribution is a speaker starting an account in response to their turning toward one another.

The section treats speaking as an act that may unfold from one utterance to another. In Moses' prayer he asks God to loosen the knot in his tongue (“واحلل عقدة من لساني”), naming an impediment to the speech he is about to deliver.
Moses' neighboring prayer asks that the people understand his speech (“يفقهوا قولي”). It connects the section's command to tell with the speaker's aim that his words be received clearly.

The section forbids a harsh verbal response to the asker. Moses and Aaron are told to speak gently to Pharaoh (“فقولا له قولا لينا”); though the addressee differs, the ayah makes gentleness a commanded way of speaking.
